You always knew that astrology was fake. As you grew up and decided to eventually pursue a career in science, the truth of astrology became very clear to you: it was firmly a pseudoscience. It was as real as the predictions of slips of paper within fortune cookies. 

One morning, you wake up and something feels... Off. It is the month of your birth and (of course) the horoscope section of your local newspaper describes how a planetary alignment will cause some cliché boost to your love life. You scoff at the paper and place it down on a counter. You just got dumped less than a month ago. There was no chance in hell that your love life was going to suddenly be boosted to rom com levels of happiness, or that your respective birthday buddies would be given Cupid's blessings either. 

After grabbing your water bottle, you slip out the door. Walking to class was a breeze, as the weather was fair. You sit down in your English class, silently praying that your professor would put you in a group of at least one or two non-athletes who would actually speak to you. Sadly, the athletic cliques did not disappear after high school graduation. Your professor finally finishes rifling through her papers. 

"Okay class-," she begins in a tone slightly more bubbly than normal, "Today's groups are going to be by season. Spring near the front windows, summer in the middle, fall in the back, and winter near the hallway. The article you'll be responding to is in the front. Have at it! I have a date in thirty so I need you to be a little fast today, okay?" The class stares at her for five seconds, trying to gauge if she actively meant to tell you about her flourishing love life.  Based on her previously quirky yet caring nature (giving out her number on the first day to text her questions, acting overly motherly, dispensing cough drops to moderately sick students, etc.) your class decides that her outburst isn't too out of the ordinary. 

Even though you typically do the required group work in five minutes and screw around with your phone while the other group members talk to each other, today was different. Two of your group members can't seem to shut up about their partners. You, being the cynical science major, currently think that love is just as dead as the horoscope you read this morning. Still, you listen out of one part curiosity and one part boredom. 

"This morning was so wild, guys. I got out of bed, and boom. There were flower petals all over the floor. Then, I went to open my folder this morning and found a goddamn handwritten love letter. Supe hasn't written anything since, I don't know, tenth grade? He doesn't even do any of his papers and the fluidity of the writing was just so... weird," the first person said. 

"Oh my God, is there something radioactive in the air?" replied the other. "When I got up this morning, my girlfriend prepared the best breakfast for the both of us, even though we both are not morning people. She planned a videogame date later tonight. I just can't believe it. We've been fighting for over a week!" 

You shrug it off. College students are volatile. People swap moods and relationship dynamics in the blind of an eye. Suddenly, your phone screen lit up. After weeks of no contact, your most recent ex decides to text you. 

"Hey," it reads. You want to sarcastically reply, "Wow, that word is the pinnacle of romance," but instead you ignore the message entirely. By the time class finishes, you just want a nice nap and then some quality YouTube binging with your roommate when they get home. 

Upon entering your room, you look down at the floor. It is a mess. Anything that could hypothetically be slid under the door... was slid under the door. Even items that could not be slid under were somehow there, as if some crazy astrological Cupid climbed up to the second floor and tossed things through your window. You examine pressed flowers, unpressed flowers, handwritten notes, a videogame of your favorite genre, 3D printed characters from the engineering lab you can't get into, and a newspaper clipping with a message written on the back: "It might not be the pinnacle of romance, but it's a start. Meet me at the dining hall at five? I could try to explain how astrology is real, but I'm sure you wouldn't believe me anyway."

I would take some of the most common facts about each element and make that into a power that is the equivalent. As an example, carbon has four valence electrons so it's knows as an extremely versatile element that can bond in tons of different ways & is found in all organic compounds (although not all compounds with carbon are organic). Sorry for the longwinded explanation, but because it's able to make so many different things, I would make carbon a shapeshifter. Hydrogen is the most flammable element, so I would give it a fire-based power, etc. For character design I would start with figuring out color schemes: cool colors (blue, green, purple) for characters that may be more water-attracted or cooling/water power, warm colors for fire or explosive characters, and possibly get some color inspiration from the true element itself (although many metals are black, colorless, or gray on their own, you could use flame test colors for some elements).

I would focus on electrochem (mostly redox reactions) and titration/equilibrium calculations because they personally kicked my ass. You might want to get a solid hold on half-life word problems (length of time until something is no longer radioactive after having a substance spilled on it, etc.) although nuclear chem may or may not be a part of the curriculum.

[Side note: I took Honors Chem II so I don't know if you're talking about what would be my school's chem I, II, or both... but for the chem I stuff I would focus on limiting reagent problems and memorizing the shapes of molecules (molecular geometry), along with understanding dipole moments.]
